title: Denatofication: Turkey’s Defense-Industrial Autonomy and the Cirit Architecture of Greater Eurasia
content: This article examines whether Turkey’s defense-industrial transformation constitutes an observable precursor to formal disengagement from NATO’s integrated military command — a process the authors term denatofication. The study addresses a gap in the strategic autonomy literature, which describes Turkey’s hedging behavior without specifying the institutional mechanism by which its structural contradiction (simultaneous NATO membership and Shanghai Cooperation Organisation aspirant status) could be resolved. Using comparative historical case study design, the article analyzes two historical precedents (France 1966–2009; Greece 1974–1980) and applies a three-dimensional sovereignty framework (infrastructural, institutional, narrative) to Turkey’s defense-industrial record from 2000 to 2026. The principal finding is that material denatofication — defense localization exceeding 80%, the sovereign Steel Dome air-defense network, the KAAN fifth-generation fighter, the Anadolu drone-carrier, and autonomous mobilization legislation — precedes and enables institutional denatofication. The Incirlik Paradox (U.S. B61 warheads; GE engines for KAAN) identifies the two residual dependencies that define the unfinished frontier of Turkish strategic autonomy. The NATO Ankara Summit (July 2026) provided real-time confirmation of both the paradox and Turkey’s structural ambivalence. Policy implications bear on NATO cohesion, SCO expansion, and Greater Eurasia architecture.
